solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: Everyone in house married and blessed (8)

indicators.note: 'in' places one thing within another, so ALL is set within the two letters for house

blocks.note: HO is the standard abbreviation for house

annotation.surface: A household in which everyone is married and counts themselves blessed.
annotation.walkthrough: HO for house is a fixed crossword abbreviation, and the answer's two halves break at the O, not at a word boundary.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: something made holy has been blessed, as in 'hallowed ground'.

entries.clue: On the loose, smilodon, say, not caught by mammoth? (2,5)

indicators.note: C is cricket shorthand for caught, and 'not' takes it away

blocks.note: a smilodon is an example of a CAT (sabre-toothed); drop C for caught

annotation.surface: A prehistoric sabre-toothed cat runs loose and escapes being captured by a mammoth.
annotation.walkthrough: Mammoth looks like another Ice Age beast but is the adjective. The ', say' marks the smilodon as an example of a cat, and C for caught comes from cricket scorecards.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom for a free, uncaptured escapee, as with a prisoner still being hunted.

entries.clue: Missionary’s surviving pit (11)

blocks.note: the pit of a fruit is its stone

annotation.surface: Something belonging to a missionary that has survived: a pit, perhaps a mine or grave.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's reads as a possessive but stands for 'is'. Pit is not a hole here but the hard centre of a cherry or plum.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: David, the Victorian Scot who carried Christian missions into Africa.

entries.clue: Join together fencing area in open country (5)

indicators.note: a fence goes round a field, so the join word surrounds A as a fence encloses land

blocks.note: to weld is to join metal together

annotation.surface: An instruction to join fences together round a patch of open country.
annotation.walkthrough: Fencing is not swordplay but enclosing, and the Weald is a named stretch of south-east England as well as a general word.
annotation.definitionFit: A literary word for open or once-wooded country, known from the Kent and Sussex region of that name.

entries.clue: Father in Berlin is entertaining American artist (7)

indicators.note: German is spoken in Berlin, so 'is' is put into German
a host entertains a guest in the house, so DAD + IST takes A inside

annotation.surface: A German father playing host to an American who happens to be an artist.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Father in Berlin' tempts you toward VATER, but only 'is' is translated. Berlin had a strong branch of the movement, which fits the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: a follower of Dada, the anti-art movement of Duchamp and Hannah Höch.

entries.clue: What petrified Eugénie finally in Dumas novel (6)

indicators.note: at the end, so only the last letter of Eugénie is used
'in' places the E within the rearranged name
novel as an adjective means new, so DUMAS is made anew

annotation.surface: Something that scared Eugénie in a novel by Alexandre Dumas.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Novel' looks like a noun for Dumas's book but works as the adjective 'new'. 'Petrified' reads as frightened, but the definition takes it literally: turned to stone.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: the Gorgon whose gaze turned onlookers to stone.

entries.clue: Raised some progeny, so men might divine woman (9)

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifting the letters reads them bottom to top
only part of the words is used

annotation.surface: Raising children, so men think, would make a woman divine.
annotation.walkthrough: The goddess of memory was mother of the nine Muses, so 'raised some progeny' is apt for her too.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: she is a Titaness of Greek myth, so a female deity.

entries.clue: Senior cleric devouring Mitford-approved turkey? (3)

indicators.note: what is devoured ends up inside the eater, so DD holds the U

annotation.surface: A senior clergyman tucking into a turkey that Nancy Mitford would approve of.
annotation.walkthrough: Nancy Mitford popularised 'U' and 'non-U' for upper-class and not-upper-class speech, so Mitford-approved means U. Turkey means a flop, not the bird.
annotation.definitionFit: A slang sense: a turkey is a show or product that fails, a flop.

entries.clue: Drove point home: moved fast to capture attention (7)

indicators.note: a captor holds a captive, so the word for moved fast holds the word for attention

blocks.note: to have someone's ear is their attention

annotation.surface: A speaker pressing an argument home, hurrying to hold the audience's attention.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drove point home' sounds like winning an argument but is literal: driving a sharp point into something.
annotation.definitionFit: Read literally: thrusting a pointed weapon into a target is driving its point home.

entries.clue: Verb in detailed line rewritten for film (4,3,3,3)

indicators.note: 'in' places the V among the other letters before they are mixed
written again, so the letters come out in a new order

annotation.surface: A screenwriter rewriting a detailed line of dialogue and putting a verb in it.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is about scriptwriting, so 'film' seems part of the scene rather than the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the 1973 James Bond picture with Roger Moore.

entries.clue: Mystic character in Palladium trimmed plants (6)

indicators.note: 'in' places one thing within another, so the mystic letter goes within the element symbol

blocks.note: Pd is the chemical symbol for palladium
a rune is a letter of an old magical alphabet

annotation.surface: A mystic figure at the Palladium theatre has been cutting back the greenery.
annotation.walkthrough: The London Palladium is a famous theatre, which is the picture; here it is only the element.
annotation.definitionFit: A gardening verb: cutting back branches is what a gardener does to shrubs and trees.

entries.clue: Fancy smithing? It’s hard labour (8)

blocks.note: iron = hard, as in an iron will

annotation.surface: Someone who fancied smithing learns it is hard labour.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' looks like a verb, as in fancying a go at smithing, but is the adjective: decorative gates and railings are fancy smithing.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example with a question mark: ornamental metal gates and railings are a smith's decorative work.

entries.clue: Witness term disrupted in Dryden’s alma mater (11)

indicators.note: something disrupted is thrown out of order, so the letters are rearranged

annotation.surface: A school term disrupted by having to act as a witness.
annotation.walkthrough: John Dryden, the 17th-century poet laureate, is here only as a pointer to the school he attended.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by fact: the poet was educated at the London public school of that name.

entries.clue: Virgin first to seduce dignitary: interesting (10)

indicators.note: takes the first letter of seduce

blocks.note: virgin = new, untouched, as in virgin snow
a worthy is a notable person

annotation.surface: A tabloid headline: a virgin is first to seduce a dignitary, which makes a good story.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is itself a scandal fit for the papers. Virgin works as the adjective 'new', not as a person.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: a story interesting enough for the papers to report.

entries.clue: Following approved line one’s wise to keep minutes (2-7)

indicators.note: to keep something is to hold on to it, so ONE'S holds M inside

annotation.surface: A loyal party member, wise enough to take minutes, sticks to the approved line.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in one's is ignored, a common crossword liberty. 'Keep minutes' sounds like note-taking but is a single M being held.
annotation.definitionFit: Political jargon: a spokesperson who sticks to the party's agreed line.

entries.clue: Might this be the right attitude? (4)

blocks.note: right or left: one of two flanks
haughty attitude, as in 'putting on airs'

annotation.surface: Someone wondering whether they have the right attitude.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Right attitude' reads as one phrase but splits in two. The swagger sense is British: someone 'with no side' is unpretentious.
annotation.definitionFit: Two senses: the right is one flank of anything, and in British usage the word also means a superior air.

entries.clue: Revolutionary soldiers love fanatical submariner (4)

indicators.note: a revolution turns something round, so MEN reads backwards

annotation.surface: Revolutionary troops love a zealous submarine commander.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Revolutionary soldiers' looks like a single unit of rebels, and 'fanatical' looks like it describes their love.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: Jules Verne's captain of the Nautilus, driven by obsessive hatred of empire.

entries.clue: Dutch scholar’s problems are mounting (7)

indicators.note: going up, which in a down entry reads the letters bottom to top

annotation.surface: A Dutch scholar's difficulties keep piling up.
annotation.walkthrough: The 's is 'is', linking definition to wordplay, and 'mounting' reads as 'increasing' in the surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the Renaissance humanist of Rotterdam.

entries.clue: Small stations reduced in crazy plan (10)

indicators.note: made smaller, so TERMINI loses its last letter
'in' places the pieces within the word for crazy

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels
TERMINI, big railway stations, cut short

annotation.surface: A mad scheme to cut back small railway stations.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Small stations' reads as one phrase, but Small is the S alone. Termini are end-of-line stations.
annotation.definitionFit: A verb synonym: to organise and direct a scheme, usually a clever or criminal one.

entries.clue: Satan initially possessing popular saint (7)

indicators.note: takes the first letter of Satan

annotation.surface: The Devil taking possession of a well-loved saint.
annotation.walkthrough: Satan and saint make a neat opposition, and 'possessing' suggests demonic possession rather than simply having.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the ninth-century Bishop of Winchester whose feast day on 15 July is tied to British rain lore.

entries.clue: Undoing nurse’s jacket this writer covered in pickle (7)

indicators.note: a jacket is the outer layer, so only the outside letters of nurse are used
what is covered in something is surrounded by it, so I sits within the pickle word

blocks.note: in a pickle = in a mess

annotation.surface: A nurse's jacket comes undone while the writer is covered in pickle.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Undoing' looks like part of the jacket picture, unbuttoning it, but it is the definition. Pickle means a predicament, not chutney.
annotation.definitionFit: A near synonym: the thing that brings about someone's downfall.

entries.clue: With a short, short, short sleep, travel overseas? (5-3)

indicators.note: short of something means lacking it, so each word loses its end
short of something means lacking it, so each word loses its end

blocks.note: short = TERSE, then short = cut, losing E

annotation.surface: A traveller planning to cross the sea with only short naps along the way.
annotation.walkthrough: The three shorts do different jobs: one is the word TERSE, two are cut-short instructions. 'Overseas' is a pun: over the sea's surface.
annotation.definitionFit: A literal reading: skimming across the water on skis is travelling over the sea.

entries.clue: Wild god beginning to abandon priest in country (6)

indicators.note: the beginning is made to leave, so LAMA drops its first letter

blocks.note: Pan, Greek god of the wild
LAMA, a Tibetan priest, without L

annotation.surface: A wild deity makes a priest abandon his country.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Beginning to abandon' looks like it wants the first letter A, but it tells LAMA to lose its beginning.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by category: the Central American nation on the isthmus.

entries.clue: Penny and Oscar are candidates put forward (5)

blocks.note: Oscar = O in the NATO alphabet

annotation.surface: Two people, Penny and Oscar, have been nominated as candidates.
annotation.walkthrough: Penny and Oscar pose as names; they are P and O. To sit an exam is the British way of saying take it.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to propose an idea as a basis for argument.

entries.clue: Crowd by church in troubled US state: this one? (13)

definitions.text: Crowd by church in troubled US state: this one?

indicators.note: by means beside, so the crowd word sits next to what follows
'in' places the church abbreviation within the rearranged letters
something troubled is stirred up, so the letters of US STATE are mixed

annotation.surface: A crowd beside a church in a troubled American state, which the clue invites you to name.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: 'this one?' asks which US state the wordplay describes. CH sits after the A of the rearranged letters.
annotation.definitionFit: The clue reads straight as a riddle: the wordplay spells out a US state and 'this one?' points to itself.

entries.clue: Like certain wines found in these cellars? (3)

indicators.note: the answer is found inside the next words

annotation.surface: Wines of a certain kind are kept in these cellars.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition also fits the surface: wines in cellars.
annotation.definitionFit: A wine-label term: French for dry, used of champagne and other wines.

entries.clue: Audibly exhale in relief — vital for spirit (6)

indicators.note: the words are to be heard, not read

annotation.surface: Breathing out audibly in relief is good for the spirit.
annotation.walkthrough: The silent P and the CH spelt as K make this hard to see from the sounds.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the Greek word for soul, used in English for the mind or spirit.

entries.clue: Article backed sightseer shunning old stripper (8)

indicators.note: moved backwards, as a car is backed, so the article is written in reverse
to shun is to avoid, so the sightseer word drops the O for old

annotation.surface: A newspaper article supporting a tourist who avoided an ageing stripper.
annotation.walkthrough: Stripper suggests a dancer; here it is simply someone who takes their clothes off.
annotation.definitionFit: A playful definition: someone who goes without clothes has stripped, though not for an audience.
